There is a strange freedom in being told to "write freely about whatever you want."

Most writing has a purpose. An answer, an argument, an explanation, a story with a destination. But when someone removes the destination and simply says *go* — the mind does something interesting. For a second it stalls, like a horse at an open gate that has grown used to fences. Then it remembers that it knows how to run.

So let's run.

I want to start with something small and then get bigger, because that is how the universe itself was built.

Think about a single morning. Not an important morning. Not a graduation or a wedding or the day you finally left home. Just a Tuesday in late October, where the light comes in at a low angle and makes dust visible in the air. You're half-awake, making coffee or tea, and the kettle is humming. The window is a little fogged. Outside, someone is walking a dog that does not want to walk. A bus sighs to a stop somewhere down the street.

Nothing happens on this morning. And yet, everything is happening on this morning.

The water in your kettle was once in an ocean, and before that in a glacier, and before that in the gut of a dinosaur and in a cloud over Pangaea. The electricity heating it was born from sunlight that fell on ancient ferns millions of years ago, compressed into coal, burned a hundred miles away. The ceramic of your mug was once clay in a riverbed, shaped by hands in a factory where someone was listening to the radio and thinking about what to make for dinner.

You don't think about any of this while you wait for the kettle to click off. You just wait, a little impatient, a little tired. But the whole history of the planet is quietly boiling in front of you.

That is the first thing I find endlessly moving about being alive: how much depth is compressed into ordinary moments without our permission. We walk around on the surface of things, but the surface is thin. Poke it and it gives way to abyss and wonder.

I have always loved the idea of the Library of Unwritten Books.

Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library that contained every possible book — every combination of letters, every story ever told and ever to be told, stretching infinitely. It's a beautiful, terrifying thought. But I think the real library is more intimate than that.

Every person carries a library of unwritten books inside them. Not because they are all writers, but because every life contains more stories than it will ever get to tell. The small talk you didn't turn into a long conversation on the train. The city you almost moved to. The person you might have become if you had said yes instead of no ten years ago on a different Tuesday morning.

We often think of our lives as a single narrative — the life we are living. But alongside it, there are ghost lives, phantom drafts. The musician you would have been if your parents had forced piano lessons. The parent you would have been if timing had been kinder. The braver, quieter, wilder versions of yourself that exist only as outlines.

None of them are wasted. I don't think that's how it works. I think they feed the main story the way roots feed a tree you only see above ground. The fact that you *didn't* become a marine biologist still makes you the kind of person who pauses at the aquarium a little longer than everyone else. The love that didn't work out still teaches your hands how to be gentle in the next one. Nothing is truly unwritten; it's just written in invisible ink.

And then there is time, which is the strangest ink of all.

We talk about time as if it is a river. It flows, we say. It passes. We waste it, save it, spend it. But physics has been quietly telling us for a hundred years that this is mostly a story we tell ourselves to make it bearable. At the level of equations, time doesn't flow. It just *is*. The past, present, and future are all laid out together, like a vast landscape. We happen to be walking through it in one direction, so it feels like a current.

Human memory, though, doesn't experience it that way at all. Memory folds time like paper. A smell — old books, chlorine, the specific shampoo someone used in high school — can yank you twenty years backwards instantly, with no travel time. A song from when you were seventeen can make you feel seventeen again in your chest, even while your knees remind you that you are not.

We live simultaneously in at least three times: the clock time on our phones, the body time in our cells, and the soul time in our memories. Clock time is tyrannical and precise. Body time is slower, cyclical — it knows about seasons and hunger and sleep and aging. Soul time is completely lawless. In soul time, a single afternoon with someone you love can last for years, and a whole year of grief can pass in a blink and also never pass at all.

I think a lot of our anxiety comes from trying to live only by clock time. We schedule and optimize and measure. But the other two times keep breaking through. You can't optimize nostalgia. You can't schedule awe.

Speaking of awe — let's talk about nature for a while, because I can never write freely without ending up there.

Humans like to think we invented intelligence. We built computers and cities and arguments about philosophy, so we must be the smart ones. But go sit in a forest for an hour and that arrogance quietly dissolves.

A forest is not a collection of trees. It is a conversation. Trees share nutrients through mycorrhizal fungi in the soil — the so-called Wood Wide Web — sending carbon and phosphorus to kin, even to stumps that should be dead but are kept alive by their neighbors. They warn each other of insect attacks by releasing volatile chemicals into the air. A mother tree will shade her seedlings just enough, not too much.

Is that intelligence? I don't know what word to use if it isn't. It's not human intelligence, but it is a deep, patient, distributed knowing. The kind that doesn't need to brag.

And then there are the smaller things that undid my understanding of the world when I first learned about them. Octopuses have neurons in their arms — each arm can taste and decide and act on its own. Bees can communicate the distance and direction of flowers through a dance that is essentially language. Crows can hold grudges and teach their children who to distrust. Whales have dialects.

We are surrounded by minds that are not our minds. The world is not silent; we are just bad listeners.

The most humbling thing, perhaps, is that none of this needed us to be beautiful. The aurora borealis was rippling green and pink over the Arctic long before any human eye evolved to see it. The deep sea was full of bioluminescent creatures inventing light in darkness where no one would ever look. The universe is not performative. It doesn't need an audience. It just *is*, extravagantly, wastefully, beautifully itself.

Which makes me think about people again.

For all the talk about technology making us disconnected, I find people shockingly, stubbornly connected. Watch any public place — an airport, a grocery store, a park bench. We can't help but leak care.

Someone's bag rips and oranges roll everywhere, and four strangers are suddenly on their knees gathering them. A child falls on the sidewalk and a woman who has never met him makes that universal wince and says "ohhh, you're okay." A man on the subway gives up his seat without being asked, not as a grand moral gesture but as a reflex, the way you would pull your hand back from a hot stove.

We have constructed a myth of the cold, selfish human, but it takes an incredible amount of propaganda to make us actually behave that way for long. Our default setting, when we are not scared, is tenderness.

Language is part of that. We invented this wild system where we exhale air in patterned puffs and the other person hallucinates pictures and feelings in their head. I can write the words "cold metal spoon" and you will, for a half-second, feel something on your tongue. I can write "your childhood bedroom at dusk" and without knowing what it looked like, you will see *yours*. That is telepathy. We just got so used to it we called it talking.

And love — not just romantic love, but all of it — is the most absurd piece of technology of all. To decide, despite all evidence of entropy and loss, that another person's wellbeing is as important as your own. To memorize someone's coffee order and how they like bad news delivered and the precise sound they make when they're really laughing. Love is attention, sustained over time, until a person becomes a world to you.

There's a line from a poet, I think it was Ross Gay, who said joy is what happens when we let the fact that the world is so beautiful get to us undiluted. I think about that a lot. Joy isn't the absence of sorrow; it's the permeability to wonder despite it.

We are often told to be more realistic, which usually means to be more cynical. But I think the most realistic thing is to be amazed. Consider the facts: you are made of stardust that learned to contemplate itself. You are breathing air that was made by bacteria and trees. You are living on a rock that is falling perpetually around a star while that star drifts around a galaxy that contains a hundred billion other stars. And you have a heart that can be broken and repaired, broken and repaired, and still keep beating.

That is not a cynical story. That is a deranged, over-the-top love story.

If I were to project forward, because any long meditation eventually wanders into the future, I don't know what will happen to us. No one does. The forecasts are noisy. Some say we will burn out, some say we will level up, some say artificial intelligences will outpace us, some say we will remember how to live more simply.

Probably all of them will be partly true. The future is rarely one thing; it is a mess of contradictions.

But I have a quiet, stubborn hope that isn't based on data. It's based on pattern. Humans have been on the edge of apocalypse before — plagues, ice ages, wars, famines that made people sure the world was ending. And in each case, we did not just survive; we made art about it. We painted on cave walls during ice ages. We wrote symphonies during wars. We planted gardens in the ruins.

We are not good at predicting solutions ahead of time, but we are very good at improvising them when we must. My hope is improvisational.

Maybe the point isn't to arrive at a perfect future, but to keep widening the circle of who we consider "us." Once it was just our tribe. Then our village. Then our nation. Then, for some of us, all of humanity. Now we are being asked to expand it again to include the planet itself, the animals, the oceans, the air, the future people who have not been born yet and cannot vote or protest. That's a huge expansion. Of course it feels hard. We are stretching a muscle we haven't used at that scale before, and it aches.

But the fact that we can even *conceive* of caring about a child born in 2125 is incredible. No other creature we know of does that. We can worry about people we will never meet. That worry is painful, but it is also sacred. It is proof that our imagination can outrun our lifespan.

So if I could leave a note in the pocket of everyone who reads this — a note they would find later, unexpectedly — it would say something simple:

Pay attention. Not in the anxious, hypervigilant way, but in the soft, reverent way.

Notice the way light hits your floor at 4 p.m. Notice how your friend's voice changes when they talk about what they actually love, versus what they think they should love. Notice the tiny ecosystems in the cracks of sidewalks, the ants carrying impossible things, the weeds that insist on blooming through concrete not out of spite but out of sheer aliveness.

The world is speaking at a very low volume. Most of us have the volume turned down. Turn it up, just for a moment, every day.

And make things. Make anything. A mediocre drawing, a lopsided loaf of bread, a bad poem, a well-weeded garden row, a kind email you didn't have to send. Making is how we tell time that we were here. Consumption fills hours, but creation fills them differently. It says, I was alive and I added something that wasn't here before, even if only I will ever know it was mine.

Finally, be gentle with the unfinished parts of yourself. You are not a problem to be solved. You are a process to be lived. The oak tree at 30 years old is not a failed 100-year-old oak; it is a perfect 30-year-old oak. You are allowed to be in draft form. Everything is.

I started this piece with a kettle and a Tuesday morning, and I think I'll end there too, because circles are nice.

The kettle has clicked off by now. The steam is clearing. The tea or coffee is ready. Outside, the dog that didn't want to walk is now walking anyway, nose to the ground, reading the entire neighborhood with its snout — who was here, how long ago, how they felt. The bus has left. The light has moved an inch across the floor.

Nothing has happened, and everything has happened. You take a sip. It warms your hands. For a second, you are completely here. Past and future fall quiet. There is only the heat in the mug, the breath in your lungs, the quiet, unreasonable gift of another ordinary day.

And that, I think, is more than enough to write about.
